issues.legal_issue: A record-of-rights entry is rebuttable, and land may be proved to be a proprietor’s private land through other satisfactory evidence even without proof of twelve years’ cultivation.
material_facts: The land was recorded as being held by settled raiyats, raising a presumption that the entry was correct.
Earlier mortgage deeds and a later lease deed contained recitals supporting the land’s use as the proprietor’s private land.
The record-of-rights proceedings had no supporting evidence before the recording authority, and the parties challenging the entry produced documentary evidence in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The documentary evidence rebutted the statutory presumptions, and the land was proved to be the proprietor’s private land.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 103-B and 120(2) of the Bihar Tenancy Act, entries and the presumption against private-land status are evidentiary and rebuttable; a record-of-rights entry does not create rights. Section 120 does not make twelve years’ cultivation the exclusive means of proving private-land status: other relevant and admissible evidence may suffice. Where no evidence supported the entry before the recording authority, evidence satisfying the court may rebut it. The Court relied on Bogha Mower v. Ram Lakhan and Yakub Ali v. Muhammad Ali on rebutting record entries, and Maharaja Kesho Prasad Singh v. Parmeshri Prasad Singh and Bindeshwari Prasad Singh v. Maharaja Kesho Prasad Singh on the scope of section 120.

predicates.civil_private_land_classification: The proceeding required a court to determine whether disputed land was a proprietor’s private land.
predicates.reliable_earlier_documents_support_priva: Documents made before the dispute contained reliable recitals supporting the land’s use as the proprietor’s private land.
predicates.record_made_without_supporting_evidence: The record-of-rights entry was made without evidence supporting it being presented to the recording authority.
predicates.record_basis_shown_unreliable: The evidence showed that the materials underlying the record-of-rights entry did not justify it.

issues.definition: When a civil private-land classification dispute is supported by reliable earlier documents and the record entry lacks a reliable evidentiary basis, the land’s private status is established.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory presumption of genuineness for an old document does not apply to a certified copy, and it does not establish an alleged agent’s authority to act for another.
material_facts: The parties relied on certified copies of objection petitions said to have been filed in the record-of-rights proceedings.
The petitions purported to bear the signature of a person acting as an agent for the landowners.
There was no proof that the signatures were genuine or that the purported agent had authority to represent the landowners.
issues.conclusion: No presumption of genuineness arose for the certified copies, and no presumption established the purported agent’s authority.
issues.legal_principle: Section 90 of the Evidence Act permits a presumption of genuineness for qualifying original documents, not certified copies. It does not authorize a presumption that an agent had authority to act for another. The Court relied on Basant v. Brijraj.

rule.if: documentary_authentication_dispute and document_is_certified_copy and (signature_is_unproved or alleged_agent_authority_is_unproved)

predicates.documentary_authentication_dispute: A party relied on an old document in a dispute over whether it was authentic or properly made on another person’s behalf.
predicates.document_is_certified_copy: The document relied on was a certified copy rather than the original.
predicates.signature_is_unproved: The signature appearing on the document was not proved to be genuine.
predicates.alleged_agent_authority_is_unproved: The authority of the person who purported to sign as an agent was not proved.

issues.definition: In a documentary-authentication dispute, reliance on a certified copy or an unproved agent’s authority does not produce a statutory presumption of genuineness or authority.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant inducted by a mortgagee who is neither a proprietor nor a tenure-holder does not thereby acquire the statutory status required for occupancy rights.
material_facts: The land was found to be the proprietors’ private land and had been under their personal cultivation when mortgaged.
The tenants entered possession under a lease granted by the mortgagees, rather than under the proprietors.
The mortgagees were neither proprietors nor tenure-holders as defined by the tenancy legislation.
issues.conclusion: The tenants did not qualify as raiyats under the statutory definition and acquired no statutory occupancy rights.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(2), 5(3), 20 and 21 of the Bihar Tenancy Act require a claimant to qualify as a raiyat holding land immediately under a proprietor or tenure-holder and to satisfy the settled-raiyat requirements. A mortgagee is neither a proprietor nor a tenure-holder for that purpose, so a tenant inducted by a mortgagee does not acquire occupancy rights on that basis. The Court applied Mahabir Gope v. Harbans Narain Singh.

predicates.statutory_occupancy_claim: A tenant claimed statutory occupancy rights in a dispute over possession of land.
predicates.tenant_entered_under_mortgagee: The tenant obtained the right to hold the land from a mortgagee rather than from the proprietor or a tenure-holder.
predicates.mortgagee_is_not_proprietor_or_tenure_ho: The person who inducted the tenant held as a mortgagee and did not qualify as a proprietor or tenure-holder.

issues.definition: A tenant claiming statutory occupancy rights does not acquire them through a person who inducted the tenant as mortgagee and lacked the required status.

issues.legal_issue: A lease granted by a mortgagee, even if binding as an act of prudent management, does not itself confer permanent occupancy rights and cannot bind the owner beyond the lease’s applicable duration.
material_facts: The mortgagees granted the tenants a lease for a fixed term over the land.
The tenants remained in possession after the fixed term and the mortgage was later redeemed.
The Court assumed, without deciding, that the mortgagees could continue the tenants in possession as an act of prudent management.
issues.conclusion: Even on that assumption, the lease could give the tenants no more than a temporary tenancy and did not confer occupancy rights or a right to remain after the applicable tenancy period ended.
issues.legal_principle: Section 76(a) of the Transfer of Property Act is an exception to the rule that a person cannot confer a right greater than the one held: a mortgagee’s lease made in the course of prudent management may bind the owner, but its operation cannot extend beyond its applicable duration. If the tenants held over as tenants from year to year, their possession could not continue beyond the agricultural year in which redemption occurred. The Court rejected the broad reading of Rajendra Nath v. Dinu Prodhan, doubted and distinguished Binod Lal Pakrashi v. Kalu Pramanik, distinguished Pramatha Nath v. Sashi Bhusan, and explained that the other cited decisions did not establish that a protected mortgagee’s lease itself creates statutory occupancy rights.

predicates.possession_claim_after_mortgage_redempti: A person entitled to the property sought possession after the mortgage was redeemed.
predicates.mortgagee_granted_lease: The person in possession as mortgagee granted a lease to the occupant.
predicates.lease_was_only_temporarily_continued: The lease could bind the owner, at most, for its term or an applicable temporary tenancy period.

issues.definition: When possession is claimed after redemption, a mortgagee’s lease that continued only temporarily does not give the occupant a permanent occupancy right.
